clue.text: What the exultant cricketer might do to avoid a trying time!

definitions.text: What the exultant cricketer might do to avoid a trying time!

parts.words: What the exultant cricketer might do to avoid a trying time!
parts.note: a delighted cricketer might leap over the bails on the stumps; a defendant who skips a court date to dodge a trial does the same in another sense

explanation.surface: A celebrating cricketer leaps about, and the clue hints at a way out of a hard day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trying time' is a time being tried in court: skipping it after release on security is the offence. Bails are the two small wooden pieces that sit on top of the cricket stumps.
explanation.definitionFit: Absconding while on release pending trial is the idiom, forfeiting the money put up as surety.

clue.text: Preserve glass from tight crush and sudden shock

parts.note: a jam is a crowd packed tightly together
a jar is a jolt or jarring shock

explanation.surface: A glass container breaks in a crowd and a jolt.
explanation.definitionFit: A glass container for preserves, the fruit spread kept in the kitchen.

clue.text: Mutilate leg on which chap stands

definitions.text: Mutilate leg on which chap stands

indicators.note: in a down clue, a figure that stands is placed above, so the chap comes on top of the leg

parts.note: a man is a chap

indicators.note: to mutilate is to disfigure, so the letters of the word after it are rearranged

explanation.surface: Damaging the very limb a man is standing on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mutilate' rearranges LEG into GLE; 'stands' with 'on which' puts MAN on top of it in this down light. The whole clue is also the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To mangle is to mutilate or crush and tear, as a limb might be.

clue.text: Barrister who serves local customers?

explanation.surface: A lawyer moonlighting at a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: A barrister is a man of the Bar, the legal profession; 'local' in Britain is the neighbourhood pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Split as two words it is a man called to the legal Bar; whole, it is someone pouring drinks in a pub.

clue.text: Plea not applicable to the unemployed

explanation.surface: An appeal that does not apply to people out of work.
explanation.definitionFit: A prayer or appeal to a higher power; split as 'in vocation', it means in an occupation, which the jobless are not.

clue.text: County employees

explanation.surface: A local council's workforce.
explanation.definitionFit: Staffordshire, an English Midlands county, is abbreviated this way; a workforce is also its plural staff collectively.

clue.text: Boston riot arranged by a mad hatter

explanation.surface: Unrest in Boston, organised by an eccentric hat-maker.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1773 Boston protest dumped British tea into the harbour; the Mad Hatter hosts a tea gathering in Alice in Wonderland.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1773 Boston protest against tea duty, and the gathering hosted by Lewis Carroll's Hatter.

clue.text: Legitimate target of abuse, but it is only just sport

explanation.surface: A remark about who may rightly be criticised, and about playing fairly.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone open to attack or ridicule; read literally, a contest played honestly.

clue.text: Pair is taken in by certain unexpected event

indicators.note: taken in by means held within, so the first pieces go inside the word for certain

parts.note: sure means certain
taken as written

explanation.surface: A couple are fooled by a sure thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken in by' puts PR and IS inside SURE, after its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sudden and unforeseen is a shock or startling occurrence.

clue.text: Isle with a lot of trees or one tropical tree

parts.note: the Isle of Man, the island in the Irish Sea, gives its name
a grove is a small wood, a group of trees

explanation.surface: An island covered in woodland, or else one solitary tree of the tropics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or' is a link word here, joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a tree of tidal swamps in hot countries, growing on stilt-like roots.

clue.text: Repair broken sword

indicators.note: something broken is in pieces, so the letters of the word before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: Asking a smith to mend a damaged blade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' rearranges the letters of 'Repair'.
explanation.definitionFit: A light, slender, sharp-pointed blade used for thrusting in duelling.

clue.text: A match for the two other parties?

definitions.text: A match for the two other parties?

parts.words: A match for the two other parties?
parts.note: a match is a union, as in marriage; the clue also suggests a grouping strong enough to rival Labour and the Conservatives in British politics

explanation.surface: Someone proposes a suitable pairing to two outsiders.
explanation.walkthrough: In the 1980s the Liberal and SDP partnership in Britain was known by this name, positioned as the third force against the two main parties.
explanation.definitionFit: A union or pact is a match in the sense of joining together; the Liberal-SDP grouping took this title.

clue.text: Could the proverbial dog in it get a dog ailment right after?

definitions.text: Could the proverbial dog in it

indicators.note: after places the letter for right behind the ailment

parts.note: mange is a skin disease of dogs caused by mites

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the dog in the famous saying might catch a canine skin complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'dog in the manger' is someone who spitefully keeps from others what they cannot use themselves; the clue asks what the dog lies in.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb has a dog lying in a feeding trough for cattle, refusing to let them eat the hay.

clue.text: Union policy which serves no customer

explanation.surface: A trade union rule that turns everyone away.
explanation.walkthrough: A trade union policy requiring all workers at a firm to be members; literally, a store not open for trade.
explanation.definitionFit: A workplace where only union members may be employed; also a store with its doors locked.

clue.text: Has another widespread daily changed its format permanently?

definitions.text: Has another widespread daily changed its format permanently?

parts.words: Has another widespread daily changed its format permanently?
parts.note: split two-three-five, the phrase reads as a newspaper that has become tall in shape; 'permanently' is the plain meaning

explanation.surface: A reader asks whether yet another national newspaper has switched its page size for good.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as 'A TALL TIMES', the phrase describes a broadsheet daily in a changed format; read normally it means always.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means always or forever, which is what 'permanently' says.

clue.text: Nothing in a Leftist slogan

parts.note: the phrase means utterly excluded, with nothing of it inside, and would also be a socialist's chant demanding the political right be expelled

explanation.surface: A remark that there is no substance in a socialist rallying cry.
explanation.walkthrough: As a phrase it means completely or entirely out; a left-winger chanting it would be calling for conservatives to go.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means wholly or completely gone, so nothing is in.

clue.text: Device recommended for company without any true organisation

definitions.text: Device recommended for company without any true organisation

parts.words: Device recommended for company without any true organisation
parts.note: a firm lacking real order would be advised to buy an electronic machine that keeps records and processes data

explanation.surface: Advice to a disorganised business to get a certain machine.
explanation.definitionFit: An electronic machine that stores and processes data, bringing system to records.

clue.text: Its avian song sounds unbelievable

parts.note: the first half of the bird's name is said like a word for someone who tells untruths, and the bird mimics other sounds so well that its song is hard to believe

explanation.surface: A remark that a bird's song is incredible.
explanation.walkthrough: This Australian bird mimics chainsaws and camera shutters; its first word is said like 'liar', which fits a song that sounds unbelievable.
explanation.definitionFit: An Australian ground bird famous for mimicking other sounds; its tail is shaped like a lyre.

clue.text: African state which also boasts of its trunk-roads

definitions.text: African state which also boasts of its trunk-roads

parts.words: African state which also boasts of its trunk-roads
parts.note: elephant tusks are the material from an elephant's mouth, near its trunk, and a coast is a shoreline route; the hyphenated pair plays on main roads

explanation.surface: A West African nation brags about its highway network.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trunk-roads' in Britain are main highways; here 'trunk' points to elephants and their tusks, the trade that gave this West African country its name.
explanation.definitionFit: Côte d'Ivoire, the West African republic, is known in English by this name from its old trade in elephant tusks.

clue.text: Display article and make merry about it

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for make merry goes around the article

parts.note: to revel is to make merry
A is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Putting on a show of an item and celebrating around it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts REVEL around A.
explanation.definitionFit: To display is to show or disclose something to view.

clue.text: Best sort of penalty is imposed on a pious man

indicators.note: imposed on places the penalty on top of the saint in this down clue

parts.note: a fine is a kind of penalty paid in money
ST is the abbreviation for saint, a holy person

explanation.surface: A penalty slapped on a devout person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is imposed on' puts FINE above ST in this down light.
explanation.definitionFit: Of the highest quality, the very top superlative.

clue.text: Camera shot on a pole needs a little bit of light

indicators.note: on means placed above, as this is a down light

parts.note: a photo is a picture taken with a camera
N is north, one of the two poles

explanation.surface: Taking a photograph on a pole requires a small amount of light.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' puts PHOTO above N in this down light; 'needs' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A quantum or particle of electromagnetic radiation, the smallest unit of illumination.

clue.text: Locust fed with grain by the farmer

definitions.text: fed with grain by the farmer

explanation.surface: An insect pest raiding a farmer's corn supply.
explanation.definitionFit: A grasshopper or locust is called by this name; it is also the funnel-shaped container a farmer fills with seed or feed.

clue.text: Do they just leave their money to work for them?

definitions.text: Do they just leave their money to work for them?

parts.words: Do they just leave their money to work for them?
parts.note: people who live off investments do no labour themselves, letting their wealth earn

explanation.surface: A question about wealthy folk letting their capital do the work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work for them' is turned around: the wealthy themselves stay inactive while their capital earns interest.
explanation.definitionFit: Wealthy people who live without working, on inherited or invested funds, are described this way.

clue.text: Beefeater's favourite soup

parts.note: a Beefeater is a Yeoman Warder at the Tower of London, but the word read literally is someone who eats beef, who would like a soup made from cattle

explanation.surface: Asking which soup the Tower of London guards prefer.
explanation.walkthrough: Beefeaters are the ceremonial guards at the Tower of London; read literally, the word means a meat eater, who would enjoy a soup made from part of a bullock.
explanation.definitionFit: A thick soup is made from the tail of a cow or bullock, which suits someone who eats beef.

clue.text: Stop giving advice to the farmer whose milk has gone sour

definitions.text: giving advice to the farmer whose milk has gone sour

explanation.surface: Someone tells a dairy farmer what to do with spoilt milk.
explanation.definitionFit: Old slang for 'stop it' or 'clear off'; also literal advice to turn soured milk into curds.

clue.text: Long speech for one in business

indicators.note: in places the numeral for one inside the word for business

parts.note: trade is commerce, business
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A lengthy address on behalf of someone in commerce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts I inside TRADE; 'for' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A long, angry, critical address is a harangue of this kind.

clue.text: Physicist tells what struck Newton with great weight

parts.note: legend says a falling apple hit Isaac Newton and inspired his theory of gravity
a ton is a large unit of weight

explanation.surface: A scientist describes what fell on Newton's head and how heavy it felt.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Edward Appleton was a British physicist who won the 1947 Nobel Prize for research on the ionosphere.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Appleton, Nobel laureate who discovered the ionospheric layer named after him.
